worst_disagreements.feedback: The idea of the proof is correct, but the inequality $B+1 \geq B$ is insufficient to prove the point to be shown (we need $B+1 > B$). While fixing this is easy, the proof does also not show why precisely there is no upper bound of the natural numbers in the reals. This is not trivial, since there are non-archimedean ordered fields where indeed the natural numbers are bounded above.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
0/5  
• The answer contains no correct or relevant argument toward showing that ℕ is not bounded above in ℝ.  

1/5  
• The student merely states that the natural numbers “go on forever” or “are infinite,” but gives no clear link to the formal definition of “bounded above” or no explanation of how that infinity contradicts boundedness.  

2/5  
• The answer recognizes that to show “not bounded above” one must, for an arbitrary real M, produce a natural number exceeding M—but fails to exhibit such a construction or to justify its existence rigorously.  

3/5  
• The student proposes a candidate (for example n = ⌊M⌋+1) that indeed exceeds M, but does not justify why ⌊M⌋ is a well‐defined natural number or appeals to the floor function or integer part without validation.  

4/5  
• The proof correctly invokes the Archimedean property (“for every real M there is n∈ℕ with n>M”) and applies it to conclude that ℕ has no real upper bound, but treats the Archimedean property as a given fact without proof or reference to foundational axioms.  

5/5  
• A fully rigorous, self‐contained proof based only on the axioms/assumptions provided. For example: assume for contradiction that ℕ were bounded above, let s=sup ℕ, use the completeness axiom to derive that there is some natural k satisfying s–1<k≤s, then note k+1∈ℕ yet k+1>s, a contradiction. Equivalently, prove (or cite a proved version of) the Archimedean property from the axioms and then show directly that for any real M one constructs n∈ℕ with n>M, so no upper bound exists.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your core idea—that assuming a maximal natural number leads to a contradiction via \(B+1\in\Bbb N\)—is perfectly valid for showing “there is no largest element” in \(\Bbb N\). What’s missing is the link to the formal notion of “bounded above in \(\Bbb R\).” In particular:

1. Recall the definition: “\(\Bbb N\) is bounded above” means there exists some real \(M\) such that for every \(n\in\Bbb N\), \(n\le M\).  
2. You should begin by assuming such an \(M\) exists, then either:  
   a. Exhibit an explicit \(n\in\Bbb N\) with \(n>M\) (for example \(n=\lfloor M\rfloor+1\) or simply \(n=\lceil M\rceil\)), or  
   b. Use completeness: let \(s=\sup\Bbb N\), find \(k\in\Bbb N\) with \(s-1<k\le s\), then observe \(k+1>s\).  
3. Conclude that no real \(M\) can bound \(\Bbb N\) from above.

By spelling out the definition of “bounded above” and showing directly how any putative bound \(M\) fails, you close the logical gap.

   – For the lower bound, shows that if (m,n) is an integer point with m²+n² ≤ (R−√2)² then the entire unit square [m−½,m+½]×[n−½,n+½] lies in the disk of radius R, so f(R) ≥ area of disk radius (R−√2) = π(R−√2)².  
   – For the upper bound, shows conversely that every point of the disk of radius R lies in some square [m−½,m+½]×[n−½,n+½] centered at a lattice point (m,n), and that each such square is contained in the disk of radius R+√2, giving f(R) ≤ area of disk radius (R+√2) = π(R+√2)².

Your proof shows that you know the right overall idea (comparing the disk to unit-squares around lattice points), but both of your inclusion arguments are too imprecise or mixed up.  Here’s how to tighten them:

1.  Cleanly separate the two bounds.  Label them “Lower bound” and “Upper bound.”

2.  Lower bound (π(R–√2)² ≤ f(R)):  
   –  Start by assuming an integer point (m,n) satisfies m² + n² ≤ (R–√2)².  
   –  Show that every point (x,y) in the closed square [m–½, m+½]×[n–½, n+½] still lies inside the disk of radius R.  
     •  Use the fact that the farthest any point in that square can be from its center (m,n) is the half-diagonal, √2⁄2, so  
       |(x,y)| ≤ |(m,n)| + √2⁄2 ≤ (R–√2) + √2⁄2 < R.  
   –  Conclude that each such square is fully contained in the disk, so counting those squares gives f(R) ≥ area of disk radius (R–√2) = π(R–√2)².

3.  Upper bound (f(R) ≤ π(R + √2)²):  
   –  Take any point (x,y) in the disk of radius R.  It lies in some unit-square centered at an integer lattice point (m,n).  
   –  Show that if (x,y) lies in that square, then its center (m,n) must satisfy m² + n² < (R + √2)²: again the maximum extra distance from center to a corner is √2⁄2, so  
       |(m,n)| ≤ |(x,y)| + √2⁄2 < R + √2⁄2 < R + √2.  
   –  Therefore every such square is contained in the disk of radius R+√2, so the total number of squares f(R) cannot exceed the area π(R+√2)².

4.  Watch your inequalities and constants very carefully (e.g. use “≤” vs “<” consistently, and note that the half-diagonal is √2/2, not √2).  Finally, say explicitly that each unit square has area 1, so the count of squares is exactly the area of their union, which you compare against π(R±√2)².

worst_disagreements.prompt:
\ $N(>2)$ dogs are equidistantly distributed on the circumference of a circle of radius $R$. Suddenly, at $t = 0$, the dogs enter a race where each chases his nearest (counter-clockwise) neighbour. Assume that for $t > 0$ each dog runs at a constant speed $v$ at a heading always directly towards its neighbour.
Will the dogs ever catch up with each other? If so, what distance will they traverse before
doing so?
worst_disagreements.output:
\begin{proof}
Due to the dogs being equidistant from each other, we use the symmetry principle to determine that the position of the dogs will form an equilateral triangle of which the center will be the center of the original circle since the dogs will stay equidistant due to symmetry and distance from the center will be the same for all the dogs. \\
From this, we see the dogs will meet at the center if they do indeed meet. We now only need to consider the distance each dog is from the center. \\
Since each dog is travelling at speed $v$ towards each other, we take the component of speed in the direction of the center. \\
Due to results from Trigonometry, this is $\frac{v \sqrt{3}}{2} $.
Our speed is constant, so time until dogs reach the center is $\frac{2R}{v \sqrt{3}}$
\end{proof}
worst_disagreements.feedback: Elements of a correct solution are there, i.e. the notion that symmetry properties of the problem allow us to conclude that the configuration of the $N$ dogs will always be a regular $N$-gon and that describing the motion in polar coordinates shows that the $N$-gon shrinks at a constant rate dependent only on the angular separation of the dogs and speed (hence only on $N$ and $v$), showing both convergence to the center and time/distance to convergence. However, these arguments are not clearly laid out in the proposed solution and the solution only treats the case $N=3$.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
Here is a suggested five‐point mark scheme (0–5) for the pursuit‐curve problem.  At each level we indicate the minimal evidence required in a student’s write‐up.

0 / 5  
· Response shows no correct logical steps toward solving the problem.

1 / 5  
· States (perhaps correctly) that the dogs spiral inwards or will meet, but gives no quantitative or geometric argument.

2 / 5  
· Recognizes that each dog’s velocity vector makes a constant angle of π∕N with the radius (or with the tangent), and so the motion is along a logarithmic spiral; or writes down an informal “spiral‐in” differential relation without carrying it through.

3 / 5  
· Correctly resolves the constant‐speed vector v into radial and tangential components, e.g.  
 dr/dt = −v cos(π∕N),  
(and/or dθ/dt = v sin(π∕N)/r),  
and states the ODE in a form ready for integration.

4 / 5  
· Carries out the integration of dr/dt = −v cos(π∕N) to obtain the meeting time  
 T = R∕(v cos(π∕N))  
and hence the total distance  
 D = v T = R∕cos(π∕N),  
but with only a brief or partly informal justification of the constant‐angle fact.

5 / 5  
· A fully rigorous solution, based only on the given assumptions:  
 • shows that the dogs remain at the vertices of a shrinking regular N‐gon,  
 • proves that the velocity of each dog bisects the interior angle and hence makes angle π∕N with the radius,  
 • sets up the exact ODE dr/dt = −v cos(π∕N), integrates from r(0)=R to 0,  
 • deduces T = R/(v cos(π∕N)) and D = vT = R/ cos(π∕N),  
with clear, logically ordered steps throughout.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your write-up makes the strong but unfounded assumption that the dogs always form an equilateral triangle – in fact the problem is posed for a general regular N-gon, so “equilateral triangle” only holds when N=3. To earn full credit you would need to:

 1. Show by symmetry that the dogs remain at the vertices of a shrinking regular N-gon (not just an equilateral triangle).  
 2. Prove that each dog’s velocity vector bisects the interior angle of that N-gon, hence makes the fixed angle π/N with the outward radius.  
 3. Resolve v into its radial component dr/dt = –v cos(π/N) and set up the ODE for r(t).  
 4. Integrate from r(0)=R down to r(T)=0 to get T = R/(v cos(π/N)) and thus D = v T = R/ cos(π/N).  

In your solution you only treated the N=3 case without justification, used a trig “result” rather than proving the constant angle, and never derived the general distance D.  To improve, replace the special-case equilateral triangle argument by the general N-gon shrinking argument, justify the angle π/N rigorously, set up and integrate the ODE, and state the final formula D = R/ cos(π/N).

worst_disagreements.prompt:
\ $N(>2)$ dogs are equidistantly distributed on the circumference of a circle of radius $R$. Suddenly, at $t = 0$, the dogs enter a race where each chases his nearest (counter-clockwise) neighbour. Assume that for $t > 0$ each dog runs at a constant speed $v$ at a heading always directed towards its neighbour.
Find the path $r(\theta)$ of the dogs.
worst_disagreements.feedback: The solution correctly begins to set up the problem as an ODE in polar coordinates. However, when doing so, an error in calculation causes a factor $-r$ to be dropped from the final ODE, which then leads to a wrong and simpler closed solution.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
Below is a 0–5 mark‐scheme tailored to the above “N dogs on a circle” chase problem.  Each bullet describes the key achievement level for that mark.

0 / 5  
• No correct logical steps towards the solution.  (For example, random remarks about circles or dogs with no attempt at modelling.)

1 / 5  
• Makes an observation (e.g. “the dogs spiral inward”) but writes down no equations or geometric reasoning to support it.

2 / 5  
• Begins to set up a kinematic relation—for instance writing something like dr/dt∼v—but fails to identify and use the two components (radial and tangential) or never links dr/dt to dθ/dt.

3 / 5  
• Correctly identifies that in polar coordinates dr/dt=–v cos(π/N) and r dθ/dt= v sin(π/N) (or equivalent) but then either (a) makes an algebraic slip in forming dr/dθ or (b) integrates wrongly or omits the integration constant, yielding an incorrect r(θ).

4 / 5  
• Derives the ODE dr/dθ= –r cot(π/N) and integrates to get r(θ)=C e^{–θ cot(π/N)}, then uses the initial condition r(0)=R to set C=R.  May, however, gloss over the justification that the pursuit‐angle π/N is constant by symmetry.

5 / 5  
• Full, rigorous derivation based strictly on the given assumptions:  
  – Uses rotational symmetry to show each dog sees its neighbour at a fixed bearing of π/N.  
  – Writes dr/dt=–v cos(π/N) and r dθ/dt=v sin(π/N).  
  – Forms and solves dr/dθ= (dr/dt)/(dθ/dt)=–r cot(π/N), integrates with constant from r(0)=R.  
  – Concludes correctly that the path is the logarithmic spiral  
     r(θ)=R exp[–θ cot(π/N)].  
  – All steps clear, justified, and no reliance on unstated assumptions.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your setup shows the right idea of decomposing velocity in polar components, but the key slip is that the tangential speed is v sin(π/N) = r · θ̇, not simply θ̇. As a result you’ve lost the factor r in dθ/dt and ended up with dr/dθ=–tan(π/N) instead of the true ODE dr/dθ=–r cot(π/N). 

To improve:

1.  Write out both polar‐coordinate components correctly:
    – radial: dr/dt=–v cos(π/N),  
    – tangential: r dθ/dt= v sin(π/N).  
2.  Solve for θ̇= (v sin(π/N))/r and form  
    dr/dθ= (dr/dt)/(dθ/dt)= –v cos(π/N) ÷ [v sin(π/N)/r] = –r cot(π/N).  
3.  Integrate dr/r=–cot(π/N) dθ ⇒ ln r= –θ cot(π/N)+const ⇒ r(θ)=R e^{–θ cot(π/N)}.  
4.  Justify that the bearing π/N stays constant by symmetry, and apply the initial condition r(0)=R to fix the constant.

worst_disagreements.prompt:
Show that the number $0$ does not have a predecessor in $\mathbb{N}$ assuming only the Peano axioms and the definition of a predecessor: $x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x$ is a predecessor of $y$ if $\nu(x) = y$.
The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
worst_disagreements.feedback: Proof correct. More mathematical rigor would be expected. For example: assume $n$ is a predecessor of $0$, then by the definition of predecessor, $\nu(n)=0$, which contradicts Peano axiom 3.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
Here is a suggested 0–5 mark scheme for the question “Show that 0 has no predecessor in ℕ under the Peano axioms, given that x is a predecessor of y iff ν(x)=y”:

0 / 5  
• The answer contains no correct logical steps toward showing 0 has no predecessor. It may be entirely off-topic, or confused about what is to be shown.

1 / 5  
• Some mention of “predecessor” or “successor” appears, but the student either misstates the definition or does not connect it at all to the Peano axioms. There is no invocation of the critical axiom (P3).

2 / 5  
• The student correctly recalls the definition “x is a predecessor of y iff ν(x)=y,” but they do not cite or correctly apply any Peano axiom (in particular P3). They may assert “obviously 0 has no predecessor” without justification from the axioms.

3 / 5  
• The answer identifies Axiom (P3) (“there is no n with ν(n)=0”) as relevant, but the final logical bridge—“hence no x with ν(x)=0, so by the definition 0 has no predecessor”—is only sketched or implicit. The student hasn’t fully spelled out the contradiction or structured it clearly.

4 / 5  
• A clear argument is given: “Assume, for contradiction, that 0 has a predecessor x, so ν(x)=0. This contradicts (P3). Therefore 0 has no predecessor.” The definition of predecessor is used explicitly, and P3 is correctly applied. The solution is essentially complete but may lack a formal “suppose … then … contradiction” framing or an explicit statement that no other axioms were needed.

5 / 5  
• A fully rigorous proof, relying only on the given definition and Axiom (P3):  
  1. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that ∃x∈ℕ such that ν(x)=0.  
  2. By the definition of “predecessor,” this x would be a predecessor of 0.  
  3. This contradicts Peano Axiom (P3), which states that no element maps to 0 under ν.  
  4. Hence no such x exists, so 0 has no predecessor.  
  The proof is logically watertight, cites exactly the assumptions used, and does not invoke any extraneous axioms.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof correctly points to Axiom (P3), but it is too terse and doesn’t explicitly invoke the definition of predecessor or exhibit the usual “assume for contradiction…” structure. To improve:

1. State the definition you’re using: “By definition, x is a predecessor of y if and only if ν(x)=y.”  
2. Introduce the proof idea clearly, e.g.  
   • “Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that 0 has a predecessor x. Then by definition ν(x)=0.”  
3. Point out the contradiction with P3: “But Axiom (P3) says there is no n with ν(n)=0.”  
4. Conclude unambiguously: “Therefore no such x exists, so 0 cannot have a predecessor.”  

These steps make the logical flow transparent and show exactly how the definition and Axiom (P3) combine to give the result.

worst_disagreements.feedback: Seems like an attempt to use (P5) but the set is not defined and the rest of the proof does not make sense.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
0/5  
• The “solution’’ contains no correct logical steps toward proving that \(x+y=0\) forces \(x=0\) and \(y=0\). It may state the conclusion but gives no valid argument from the Peano axioms or the definition of addition.

1/5  
• Contains a single correct observation (for example, correctly quoting \(x+0=x\) or noting that no natural number has successor equal to 0), but does not connect these facts into any argument that \(x+y=0\) implies \(x=0\) and \(y=0\).

2/5  
• Makes use of the recursive definition \(x+\nu(y)=\nu(x+y)\) to note that any sum involving a successor is again a successor, so \(\nu(u)\neq0\) by (P3).  
• However, the student stops short of framing this as an inductive proof or fails to show how this observation forces \(x=0\) (or \(y=0\)) in the original equation.

3/5  
• Attempts an induction argument (say, on \(x\)):  
  – Correctly proves the base case: if \(0+y=0\) then by \(x+0=x\) one deduces \(y=0\).  
  – Sketches an induction step by writing \(\nu(n)+y=\nu(n+y)\) and invoking (P3).  
• But misses one of: a clear inductive hypothesis, a precise contradiction for \(\nu(n)+y=0\), or the final inference that “no nonzero \(x\) can occur,” so the proof remains incomplete or sloppy.

4/5  
• Develops a near-complete proof by induction on \(x\):  
  1. Base case: \(0+y=0\implies y=0\) via \(x+0=x\).  
  2. Inductive step: assume \(n+y=0\implies n=0\) and \(y=0\); then \(\nu(n)+y=\nu(n+y)=\nu(0)\), contradicting (P3).  
  3. Concludes \(x\) must be 0.  
• To finish, correctly invokes commutativity \(x+y=y+x\) and the base‐case argument again to deduce \(y=0\).  
• Omits one minor detail (e.g.\ not naming (P3) explicitly in the contradiction, or not explaining why commutativity is allowed), but the logical skeleton is entirely there.

5/5  
• Presents a fully rigorous, self-contained proof entirely from the given axioms:  
  1. States clearly that one proceeds by induction on \(x\subseteq\Bbb N\) using (P5).  
  2. Base case: from \(0+y=0\) and the axiom \(x+0=x\) deduces \(y=0\).  
  3. Inductive step: assuming \(n+y=0\implies n=0\), then  
     \(\nu(n)+y=\nu(n+y)=\nu(0)\). By (P3) no successor equals 0, so \(\nu(n)+y\neq0\); hence the case \(x=\nu(n)\) cannot occur.  
     Thus the only solution is \(x=0\).  
  4. By commutativity of addition one rewrites \(x+y=0\) as \(y+x=0\) and repeats the base-case argument to conclude \(y=0\).  
  5. Each step is clearly justified by the appropriate Peano axiom or the given definition of addition, with no hidden assumptions.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your write-up shows you know the two key facts  
  (i)  x+ν(y)=ν(x+y) and Peano axiom (P3) (“no successor is 0”),  
  (ii) x+0 = x.  
However you never weave them into a coherent proof that “if x+y=0 then x=0 and y=0.”  In particular you need to:

1.  **Organize your argument**.  A standard approach is by induction (say on y):  
    – Base case y=0: from x+0=0 you get x=0.  
    – Induction step: assume for y=n the only solution of x+n=0 is x=0 and n=0; then for y=ν(n) you have  
       x+ν(n)=ν(x+n),  
       which by (P3) ≠0, so there is no solution with y=ν(n).  

2.  **Conclude** that the only possibility is y=0 and hence x=0.  Finally invoke commutativity to swap roles of x,y and repeat the base-case argument to deduce y=0 when x=0.

3.  **Cite axioms explicitly** at each step: use (P5) for your inductive proof, use x+0=x when proving the base case, use x+ν(y)=ν(x+y) and (P3) in the inductive step, and state clearly why no other case is possible.

By spelling out these steps—base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step, and final commutativity argument—you will have a fully rigorous proof.

worst_disagreements.markscheme:
Below is a six‐point rubric (0–5) for grading a proof of “for all x,y∈ℕ, x+y=y+x” using only the Peano axioms and the recursive definition of addition.

0 / 5  
• The student’s write-up contains no valid forward progress toward commutativity: e.g. merely states the result, gives an unrelated argument, or makes unjustified assertions.

1 / 5  
• There is at least a recognisable attempt to mention Peano axioms or induction, but no coherent base case or inductive step is given.  
• For instance, simply quoting “by induction” without checking x+0=0+x, or writing “assume it holds” but never proving anything.

2 / 5  
• The student correctly states and verifies the base case x+0=x=0+x.  
• They may then assert an inductive hypothesis “assume x+y=y+x” but fail to carry out or omit essential details of the inductive step (e.g. never write down x+S(y) or never relate it back to S(y)+x).

3 / 5  
• Both base case and an inductive step are presented with some substance:  
  – Base case: x+0=x and separately 0+x=x.  
  – Hypothesis: assume x+y=y+x.  
  – They write x+S(y)=S(x+y) by definition.  
• However they stop there or merely state “=S(y+x)=y+S(x)” without justifying the passage S(x+y)=S(y+x) (i.e. no mention of applying the hypothesis inside S(–)), or they fail to recall the definition of y+S(x).

4 / 5  
• The proof is structurally complete:  
 1. Base case: x+0=x and 0+x=x by definition.  
 2. Induction hypothesis: x+y=y+x.  
 3. Inductive step:  
    a) x+S(y)=S(x+y) (by recursive definition).  
    b) =S(y+x) (by IH).  
    c) =y+S(x) (by the definition of addition on the second argument).  
• What is missing for full rigor is an explicit invocation of the induction axiom (P5) or a brief remark on why we may conclude “for all y” once the step is done.

5 / 5  
• Fully rigorous, uses only Peano axioms and the recursive rules:  
 1. Clearly states what to prove: ∀x,y. x+y=y+x.  
 2. Proves the base case y=0:  
    – x+0=x by definition, and 0+x is also x (since one checks it via induction or notes the symmetric definition).  
 3. States the induction principle (from P5) on y.  
 4. Assumes as IH: x+y=y+x.  
 5. Shows  
    a) x+S(y)=S(x+y) by the recursive definition of addition,  
    b) =S(y+x) by IH,  
    c) =y+S(x) by the definition of “+” on successors.  
 6. Concludes by P5 that the property holds for all y, and since x was arbitrary, for all x,y.  
• All steps are justified by naming either a Peano axiom or the recursive law for addition, and the structure of the argument explicitly appeals to mathematical induction.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof contains all the key ideas—proving 0 + x=x, then inducting on y to get x+S(y)=S(y)+x, and even handling the “swap” inside the successor by a second little induction.  To push it up to a fully crisp Peano‐style write-up, you might:

1.  Organize it as a single induction on y (for an arbitrary but fixed x):  
    – State explicitly: “Fix x∈ℕ.  We prove P(y): x+y=y+x for all y by induction on y (axiom P5).”  
    – Base case y=0:  
       •  x+0=x by definition of +.  
       •  0+x=x by the lemma you already proved (your S₂ argument).  
    – Inductive step: assume x+y=y+x (IH).  Then  
       a) x+S(y)=S(x+y) by the recursive law.  
       b) =S(y+x) by the IH.  
       c) =y+S(x) by the same recursive law (since you already know 0+x=x, you can apply the law to compute y+S(x)).  

2.  Refer to the Peano induction axiom (P5) when you conclude “∴ P(y) holds for all y.”  Likewise, when you prove 0+x=x for all x, say “by P5 on the set S₂.”

3.  Avoid nested unnamed sets.  Define your proposition P(y) clearly, then do one clean induction.  If you really need the little lemma 0+x=x first, label it “Lemma 1,” prove it by a short induction on x, and then invoke it in the main proof.

4.  At each step, name the principle you use: e.g. “by the recursive definition of +,” “by the induction axiom P5,” or “by injectivity (P4)” if you ever cancel successors.

With these changes you will have a single, transparent induction, every use of an axiom or definition explicitly cited, and a clear flow from “base case” through “inductive step” to “for all y.”

worst_disagreements.prompt:
Show that, for all $x,y$ in $\mathbb{N}$, $(x+y)\cdot z=x\cdot z+y\cdot z$ using only recursive definitions of addition and multiplication and Peano axioms as well as commutativity of addition and multiplication. %(Distributivity law)
The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
Addition is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x + 0 = x$ and $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x + \nu(y) = \nu(x+y)$\\
Multiplication is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot 0 = 0$ and  $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot \nu(y) = x \cdot y + x$.
worst_disagreements.output:
\begin{proof}
Let $S = \{ (x,y,z); (x+y) * z = x*z + y *z\}$
$(0,0,0) \in S$ trivially. \\
For x:
If $(x,y,z) \in S$, $(\nu(x) + y) * z = \nu(x + y) * z = z * \nu (x + y) $ (by commutativity of * and +) $ = z * (x+y) + z = \nu (x) * z + y * z$. So $(\nu(x),y,z) \in S$ \\
For y:
This follows from above due to commutativity of +, thus $(x, \nu(y), z) \in S$. \\
For z:
$(x + y) * \nu(z) = (x + y) * z + x + y = x * \nu (z) + y * \nu(z)$ so $(x,y,\nu(z)) \in S$.
Defining $S_1, S_2, S_3 $as$ S = (S_1, S_2, S_3)$, we see $\forall x,y,z \in \mathbb{N}, (x+y) * z = x*z + y*z $
\end{proof}
worst_disagreements.feedback: The student is correctly trying to use (P5) for an induction on $x$. The set $S$ is not defined correctly. As is, it is a subset of $\mathbb{N}^3$: induction is over $\mathbb{N}$. Some steps are hard to follow. For example the fact that $z\star(x+y)+z=\nu(x)\star z+ y\star z$ is not immediate: it follows from the induction hypothesis and commutativity of addition. The remaining induction over $y$ and $z$ are superfluous.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
0 / 5  
• The submission contains no valid steps toward proving distributivity. It may restate the goal or quote unrelated properties but shows no correct logical argument or use of the recursive definitions.  

1 / 5  
• The student acknowledges that one should use induction or the Peano axioms but does not actually carry out a base‐case check or formulate a proper induction hypothesis. There is no progression from the assumptions toward the result.  

2 / 5  
• A correct base case is given (typically checking z = 0), but the induction step is either only sketched or simply asserts the desired conclusion “by induction” without exhibiting the inductive hypothesis or using it to derive (x+y)·ν(z). The solution may also illegitimately invoke distributivity as already known.  

3 / 5

May skip an explicit citation of P4 or P3 when ruling out impossible equalities, or omit stating the induction axiom (P5) in full, but the logical flow is essentially complete and rigorous.

• The solution contains no relevant or correct steps toward solving the problem (for example, random remarks about circles or eliminations that do not connect to proving the survivor’s label is 1).

1/5  
• The student shows only a superficial understanding of the elimination process (e.g. describes who is eliminated, or computes small cases numerically), but provides no clear statement of an inductive hypothesis, no base case verification, and no logical path to the general result.

2/5  
• The student correctly observes that the problem can be approached by induction and perhaps verifies the base case (n = 1), but either fails to set up a proper inductive hypothesis for 2^k people or does not demonstrate how the 2^(k + 1)-person case reduces to the 2^k-person case. The argument is incomplete or contains unjustified leaps.

3/5  
• The student states and verifies the base case (n = 1), formulates an inductive hypothesis that “for 2^k people the survivor is #1,” and attempts the inductive step. They correctly describe how, after the first round of eliminations in the 2^(k + 1)-case, one is left with 2^k people whose labels have been shifted, but they omit either a clear relabeling argument or a rigorous justification that the reduction really yields the same scenario as in the hypothesis.

4/5  
• The student gives a nearly complete strong‐inductive proof:  
  – Base case n=1 is checked.  
  – Inductive hypothesis: for some k≥1, the survivor among 2^k people is person #1.  
  – In the 2^(k+1) case, they show explicitly that after eliminating every second person you get 2^k survivors whose labels can be relabeled 1,…,2^k in a way that preserves the elimination pattern.  
  – They then appeal to the inductive hypothesis to conclude the result.  
  – The solution is correct but may gloss over one minor justification detail (e.g. why relabeling commutes with the elimination rule).

5/5  
• A fully rigorous proof by (strong) induction built solely on the given assumptions:  
  – Clearly states and verifies the base case n=1.  
  – Formulates the inductive hypothesis for an arbitrary k.  
  – In the step to k+1, precisely describes the first elimination round removing all even‐numbered persons, constructs a bijection between the surviving labels and the set {1,…,2^k}, and proves that under this bijection the elimination proceeds exactly as in the 2^k -case.  
  – Concludes that the unique survivor in the 2^(k+1) -case corresponds to label 1, thus completing the induction with full rigor and no unstated assumptions.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your write-up captures the rough idea of “halve and apply induction,” but it skips the one critical piece: showing that after you eliminate every second person in the 2^(k+1)-case, the survivors can be re-indexed to form exactly the same problem on 2^k people. Here are some ways to strengthen your proof:

1.  State a clear base case for n=1 (i.e. 2^1=2 people).  Check by hand that eliminating every second person leaves #1.  
2.  Formulate the inductive hypothesis explicitly:
    “Assume that for some k≥1, whenever you start with 2^k people in positions 1…2^k and eliminate every second person (2,4,6,…), the unique survivor is #1.”
3.  In the 2^(k+1) step:
   –  Observe that after removing all even labels 2,4,…,2^(k+1), the survivors are exactly the odd labels {1,3,5,…,2^(k+1)−1}, of which there are 2^k.  
   –  Define a bijection φ from these odd labels to {1,…,2^k} by φ(2i−1)=i.  
   –  Check that under φ, the rule “eliminate every second person in the remaining circle” translates into the same rule on {1,…,2^k}.  
   –  Conclude by the inductive hypothesis that φ(remaining label)=1, so the original survivor was label 2·1−1=1.
4.  Wrap up by stating explicitly that this completes the induction.

By adding this relabeling argument and spelling out your base case and hypothesis, you remove the “leap” in your current inductive step.

worst_disagreements.prompt:
Show that every nonzero element in $\mathbb{N}$ has a unique predecessor in $\mathbb{N}$ assuming only the Peano axioms and the definition of a predecessor: $x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x$ is a predecessor of $y$ if $\nu(x) = y$.
The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}

worst_disagreements.markscheme:
0/5  
• The solution contains no correct or relevant application of the Peano axioms P1–P5, no mention of predecessors or successors, and no logical steps toward showing existence or uniqueness of predecessors for nonzero elements.

1/5  
• The student makes a vague reference to “successor” or “injectivity,” but does not set up any definition of predecessor, does not use P3–P5 correctly, and fails to argue existence or uniqueness in any coherent way.

2/5  
• The student defines a predecessor as “the element that maps under ν to y,” and mentions P4 (injectivity) to suggest uniqueness, but:  
  – Does not establish existence for every nonzero y (no induction or set-construction).  
  – Does not correctly exclude 0 (omits P3).  
  – The logical structure is incomplete or hand-wavy.

3/5  
• The student gives a two-part outline:  
  (i) Existence: Introduce the set A = {n ∈ ℕ ∣ ∃ x such that ν(x)=n}, shows ν(0) ∈ A, then argues “if k ∈ A then ν(k) ∈ A,” and concludes A=ℕ by P5. However, they do not properly exclude 0 from needing a predecessor, or they confuse A with ℕ \ {0}.  
  (ii) Uniqueness: Appeal to P4 to claim that if ν(x)=ν(x′)=y then x=x′.  
  This reaches the correct result but the induction (or set-argument) is only sketched and the base/base exclusion of 0 is not handled rigorously.

4/5  
• A clear proof structure:  
  • Define A = {n ∈ ℕ ∣ ∃ x ∈ ℕ such that ν(x)=n}.  
  • Show ν(0) ∈ A (so 1 ∈ A), and for all k ∈ A, ν(k) ∈ A. By P5, A=ℕ.  
  • Observe from P3 that 0 ∉ A, so A = ℕ \ {0}. Hence every nonzero y has some x with ν(x)=y.  
  • Use P4 to show that such x is unique: if ν(x)=y=ν(x′) then x=x′.  
  The proof is essentially correct, but the student may gloss over one minor justification (e.g. explicitly citing P3 to exclude 0 from A).

5/5  
• A fully rigorous, assumption-only proof:  
  1. Let A = {n ∈ ℕ ∣ ∃! x ∈ ℕ such that ν(x)=n}.  
  2. Base step: P3 implies no n maps to 0, so 0 ∉ A; P2 guarantees ν(0)∈A (and uniqueness follows from P4).  
  3. Inductive/closure step: if k ∈ A then ∃! x with ν(x)=k; then ν(k)∈A (existence via x=k, uniqueness via P4).  
  4. By P5, A ∪ {0}? or better: use the simpler A′={n|∃ x} then refine to uniqueness—either way, conclude A = ℕ\{0}.  
  5. Hence every nonzero y has a unique predecessor x.  
  All uses of P1–P5 are explicit, the set(s) are defined cleanly, and both existence and uniqueness are proved with full logical rigor.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof correctly invokes P4 to rule out two different predecessors for the same element, so the uniqueness part is fine. However, you have not shown that *every* non-zero element actually *has* a predecessor. In particular:

1. You never define or construct the set of “successors” whose elements do have predecessors.  
2. You don’t use P3 to exclude 0, nor do you use the induction axiom (P5) to prove *existence* of a predecessor for each non-zero element.

To fix this, you could:

– Define A = { n∈ℕ | ∃ x∈ℕ with ν(x)=n }.  
– Show that 0∉A by P3, and that ν(0)∈A by P2 (so 1∈A).  
– Prove that k∈A ⇒ ν(k)∈A.  
– Conclude by P5 that A=ℕ, hence A=ℕ∖{0}, so every nonzero n has some x with ν(x)=n.  
– Then restate your P4 argument to get uniqueness.

Making these steps explicit will complete the existence part and yield a fully rigorous proof.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof has the right overall idea but is too informal and omits a couple of key steps from the Peano axioms.  In particular:

1. You never *defined* π using the unique‐predecessor fact.  Begin by saying  
   “For each n≠0 let π(n) be the *unique* m with ν(m)=n.  Existence and uniqueness follow from the Peano axioms and the given fact that every nonzero has exactly one predecessor.”  

2. Injectivity must be *proved* from P4, not just assumed known.  Say:  
   “If π(a)=π(b) then ν(π(a))=ν(π(b)), so a=b by the injectivity of ν (P4).”  

3. Your surjectivity argument needs two cases (you only handled n≠0):  
   – For a general target n∈ℕ, if n=0 take m=ν(0).  By P3, ν(0)≠0 so m lies in domain of π, and π(m)=0.  
   – If n≠0 take m=ν(n); again P3 guarantees m≠0 and π(m)=n.  

4. Finally, when you assert that ν is the inverse, you should *check* both compositions on the correct domains:  
   – π(ν(n))=n for all n∈ℕ by definition of π,  
   – ν(π(m))=m for all m≠0 by definition of predecessor.  

Making those steps explicit will upgrade your argument to full rigor.

1.  Define your function explicitly.  For example, set  
   f∶ℕ→S  by  f(n)=ν(n).  
2.  Prove injectivity using P4: if f(n₁)=f(n₂), then ν(n₁)=ν(n₂), so n₁=n₂ by injectivity of ν.

Putting these steps in order gives a bijection f∶ℕ→S with S⊊ℕ, and thus ℕ is Dedekind‐infinite.

worst_disagreements.prompt:
Prove that if for $x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x+y=0$, then $x=0$ and $y=0$ using commutativity of addition, recursive definition of addition and Peano axioms;
The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
Addition is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x + 0 = x$ and $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x + \nu(y) = \nu(x+y)$\\
Multiplication is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot 0 = 0$ and  $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot \nu(y) = x \cdot y + x$.\\
worst_disagreements.feedback: The basic idea of the induction proof is there. However, the set $A$ is defined without explicit quantification over $y$, and $\nu(x) + y = \nu(x+y)$ as well as $0 + y = y$ for all $y \in \mathbb{N}$ are assumed without proof.

Here is a suggested 0–5 mark scheme for the given question.  Each bullet lists the minimal achievement at that mark:

0 /5  
• The “solution” contains no correct logical steps toward proving that x = 0 and y = 0 from x+y=0.  (E.g. random remarks about naturals, or just restating the question.)

1 /5  
• Student recognizes that Peano’s axioms (perhaps P3 or P4) are relevant, or quotes x+0=x, but makes no correct inference linking x+y=0 to x=0, y=0.  

2 /5  
• Correctly observes the base fact x+0=x and applies it to x+0=0 to conclude x=0 in the special case y=0, but fails to treat the successor‐case meaningfully (no legitimate inductive step or case‐split alongside commutativity).  

3 /5  
• Sets up (implicitly) two cases: y=0 and y=ν(y′).  
  – Base: from x+0=0 deduces x=0.  
  – Successor case: writes x+ν(y′)=ν(x+y′)=0 and invokes P3 (“no n satisfies ν(n)=0”) to conclude this case is impossible, hence y=0.  
• Concludes x=0, y=0.  
• However, the solution does not explicitly invoke commutativity to justify treating “x+…” and “…+x” symmetrically or omits reference to one of the Peano axioms in a minor but needed detail.  

4 /5  
• Fully carries out the above case‐split and uses P3 in the successor‐case to rule out ν(…) = 0.  
• Explicitly points out or proves (by induction hypothesis or separate lemma) that y cannot be a successor, so y=0, then x=0.  
• Also invokes commutativity of addition to justify symmetry (so the proof applies equally if one had started by splitting on x).  
• Minor gap remaining (e.g. a brief hand‐wave on why an inductive assumption holds, or a missing explicit appeal to injectivity P4 or to the recursive definition of + in one step).  

5 /5  
• A perfectly rigorous derivation, entirely from the given axioms and definitions, along these lines:  
  – State and prove by induction on y ∈ ℕ: “if x+y=0 then y=0 and x=0”.  
  – Base (y=0): x+0=0 ⇒ x=0 (by definition of +).  
  – Inductive step: assume for y′: if x+y′=0 then y′=0 and x=0; consider y=ν(y′), then x+ν(y′)=ν(x+y′)=0, contradicting P3; hence this case cannot occur.  
  – Conclude y=0, so x+0=0 ⇒ x=0.  
  – Point out by commutativity that an identical argument works by induction on x, showing x=0 ⇒ y=0, or simply observe symmetry.  
  – Reference P3 for “no successor equals 0”, P4/injectivity if used, the recursive definition of + at each step, and nothing beyond the given axioms.  
• The proof is fully explicit, logically complete, and cites exactly the given axioms and definitions—no unproved assumptions or hidden appeals.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Here are the main issues and how to fix them:

1. Mis-citing the axioms and misusing them  
  – You appealed to “P4” to rule out ν(k+y)=0, but in fact it is P3 (“no successor is 0”) that gives the contradiction.  
  – Always quote the exact axiom you need: if ν(n)=0 is impossible by P3, say so explicitly.

2. Flawed inductive step  
  – You tried to prove “if ν(k)+y=0 then ν(k)=0 and y=0” by showing ν(k)+y≠0, then concluding y=0.  You cannot infer y=0 from ν(k)+y≠0.  
  – Better strategy: assume ν(k)+y=0.  Then by the recursive definition x+ν(y′)=ν(x+y′) you get ν(k+y)=0, contradicting P3.  Hence that case is impossible—and so the implication vacuously holds.  (You do not need to deduce y=0 here; vacuous truth suffices to show ν(k) ∈ A.)

3. Organization via case‐split on y (or x)  
  – It is more straightforward to do induction on y:  
    • Base y=0: x+0=0 ⇒ x=0 by definition of +.  
    • Inductive step y=ν(y′): if x+ν(y′)=0 then ν(x+y′)=0, impossible by P3.  Thus that case cannot happen.  
    • Conclude y=0, then x+0=0 ⇒ x=0.  
  – Finally, invoke commutativity to see that the same argument shows x=0 ⇒ y=0, or simply point out the symmetry of the statement.

4. Be explicit about commutativity  
  – Since the problem statement asks you to use commutativity, you should either  
    a) do two parallel inductions (one on y to get y=0, then by commutativity one on x to get x=0), or  
    b) note at the end that x+y=0 implies y+x=0 by commutativity, so once you have shown that the second coordinate must be zero, the first must be zero as well.

5. Clean up your “vacuous implication” reasoning  
  – If you want to show “for all x, (x+y=0) ⇒ (…y=0…)” by induction on x, you must argue that whenever the antecedent holds you can derive the consequent.  In the successor‐case you do this by contradiction (show the antecedent can never hold), not by asserting its negation implies extra facts.

With those corrections in place you will have a fully rigorous Peano‐axiomatic proof, correctly citing P3, using the recursive definition of +, invoking commutativity, and carrying out a proper induction.

   a^k – b^k = (a–b)\,(a^{k–1} + a^{k–2}b + … + b^{k–1}).  
   Since a≡b mod n, n divides (a–b), hence n divides the product, so a^k≡b^k mod n.

worst_disagreements.prompt: Prove that for any $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, $x>0$, there exists an $n\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $nx>y$. This is called the Archimedean Property.

worst_disagreements.markscheme:
Below is a six‐point scheme (0–5) for assessing a student’s proof of the Archimedean property

“For any real x,y with x>0 there exists n∈ℕ such that n x>y.”  

0 / 5  
 No correct or relevant steps toward a proof. May state the result or definitions but gives no logical argument.  

1 / 5  
 Some awareness of the statement (e.g. mentions “multiples of x”), but no clear construction (no set S, no contradiction plan, no appeal to completeness or ordering axioms).  

2 / 5  
 Attempts a proof sketch: e.g. defines S = {n x : n∈ℕ} or assumes “if not, then n x≤y for all n,” but fails to (a) invoke the completeness axiom in any coherent way or (b) derive a genuine contradiction.  

3 / 5  
 Correct overall approach by contradiction or direct construction, and mentions a key axiom (e.g. completeness or least upper bound). However, one or more of the following is missing or flawed:  
 – non‐emptiness of S or boundedness assumption is not checked;  
 – the supremum argument is stated imprecisely (e.g. “take sup S, then sup S – x is not an upper bound, so some m x>sup S – x” but without justification);  
 – logical flow has gaps that prevent the proof from being fully closed.  

4 / 5  
 A essentially correct proof by contradiction using the completeness axiom:  
 – Defines S = {n x:n∈ℕ}, checks it is nonempty and (by the contrary assumption) bounded above by y;  
 – Invokes existence of s = sup S;  
 – Observes s – x < s so s – x fails to be an upper bound ⇒ ∃m with m x > s – x ⇒ (m+1)x > s, contradicting s as an upper bound.  
 Only minor details missing (e.g. an explicit reference to “the completeness axiom” or a one‐line justification that S≠∅).  

5 / 5  
 A fully rigorous, self‐contained contradiction proof, based solely on the given real‐number axioms (ordering and completeness):  
 – Clearly states the contradiction hypothesis (no n with n x>y).  
 – Defines S, checks S≠∅ and S is bounded above by y.  
 – Applies the least‐upper‐bound property to obtain s=sup S.  
 – Shows s – x is not an upper bound, so ∃m∈ℕ with m x > s – x, hence (m+1)x > s, contradicting s≥all elements of S.  
 – Concludes the assumption is false, so ∃n with n x>y.

1.  Avoid circular use of “ℕ is not bounded above.”  
    – You are trying to prove exactly that fact (the Archimedean property) yet you appeal to it as if already known. Instead, derive your contradiction using the completeness (least‐upper‐bound) axiom of ℝ.

2.  Define your set properly and check basic properties.  
    – Let S = { n·x : n∈ℕ }.  
    – Show at once that S≠∅ (e.g. 1·x∈S) and, under the contrary hypothesis “n·x≤y for all n,” that S is bounded above by y.

\ $N(>2)$ dogs are equidistantly distributed on the circumference of a circle of radius $R$. Suddenly, at $t = 0$, the dogs enter a race where each chases his nearest (counter-clockwise) neighbour. worst_disagreements.feedback: The solution correctly begins to set up the problem as an ODE in polar coordinates. However, when doing so, an error in calculation causes a factor $-r$ to be dropped from the final ODE, which then leads to a wrong and simpler closed solution.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your attempt shows you recognize this as a pursuit‐curve problem and try to write down a relation between the radial and angular motions. However, the setup contains a fundamental mix-up in the decomposition of the velocity and so leads to a straight‐line spiral rather than the true logarithmic spiral. In particular:

 1.  In circular pursuit each dog’s heading is always at the fixed angle α = π/N inward from the tangential direction, so  
     –  the tangential (orthoradial) speed is v sin α, not v cos α;  
     –  the inward (radial) speed is –v cos α.  
    You have interchanged these, writing ˙θ = v cos(π/N)/r instead of ˙θ = (v sin(π/N))/r and ˙r = –v sin(π/N) instead of ˙r = –v cos(π/N).

 2.  Because ˙θ = (v sin α)/r, one obtains  
        dr/dθ = (dr/dt)/(dθ/dt) = –v cos α ÷ (v sin α / r) = –r cot α.  
    Integrating yields  
        ln r = –θ cot α + constant,  
    or equivalently the logarithmic‐spiral form  
        r(θ) = R exp[–θ cot(π/N)].  

 3.  Your linear “–θ tan(π/N)” law comes from treating the angular speed as constant and mis‐assigning the velocity components. This loses the essential 1/r factor that produces the logarithm.

Next time, begin by resolving the dog’s velocity vector into its radial and orthoradial parts with the correct sine and cosine factors. Then set up  
   ˙r = –v cos(π/N),  
   r ˙θ = v sin(π/N),  
form dr/dθ correctly, and you will arrive at the expected logarithmic spiral.

Your attempt shows that you understand the overall strategy—using induction together with the recursive definitions, commutativity, and distributivity—but the execution has several gaps.  Below are some concrete points to help you tighten up the proof:

1. Choice of induction variable and framework  
   • Associativity is a statement in three variables, but you really only need to induct on one of them (standardly on z).  You ought to define a single set  
      S = { z ∈ ℕ : ∀x,y, (x⋅y)⋅z = x⋅(y⋅z) }  
     and then invoke the Peano induction axiom (P5) on that S.  Splitting into Sₓ, Sᵧ, S_z is both unnecessary and leads to confusion about which variable you are inducting on.

2. Base case (z = 0)  
   • You must start with “Take any x,y.  We check z=0:  
        (x⋅y)⋅0 = 0  by the definition of multiplication,  
        x⋅(y⋅0) = x⋅0 = 0.  
     Hence (x⋅y)⋅0 = x⋅(y⋅0).”  
   Your proof wrote “0∈Sₓ” but never clearly fixed x,y nor showed both sides reduce to 0 via the recursive definition of “⋅0=0.”

3. Inductive step  
   • State the inductive hypothesis: “Assume for some z that for all x,y, (x⋅y)⋅z = x⋅(y⋅z).”  
   • Then consider (x⋅y)⋅ν(z).  By definition of multiplication:  
        (x⋅y)⋅ν(z) = (x⋅y)⋅z + (x⋅y).  
     Now apply the inductive hypothesis to replace (x⋅y)⋅z with x⋅(y⋅z).  You get  
        = x⋅(y⋅z) + x⋅y.  
   • Next use commutativity (x⋅y = y⋅x) to rewrite x⋅y + x⋅(y⋅z) as x⋅(y⋅z) + x⋅y, and then distributivity in the form  
        x⋅(y⋅z + y) = x⋅(y⋅ν(z)).  
     This completes the inductive step.

4. Careful use of definitions  
   • Make sure each application of commutativity or distributivity is justified by your assumptions.  When you write something like  
        (y⋅x + y)⋅z = y⋅x⋅z + y⋅z  
     you have silently used associativity on y⋅x⋅z.  But you cannot assume that before proving it!  Instead, keep the factors grouped so that every step follows directly from the recursive definitions, commutativity, and the distributive law as stated.

5. Notation and logical flow  
   • Avoid mixing up successors and multiplications, e.g. writing “(x⋅ν(y))+z” instead of “((x⋅y)+x)⋅z.”  
   • Every time you invoke induction you must clearly say “by the inductive hypothesis,” and every time you use a Peano axiom or a recursive definition you should cite it (even informally) so the reader can see there’s no hidden appeal to an unproved version of associativity.

With these adjustments—one clear induction on z, fully written base case, a step-by-step inductive proof relying only on the given definitions and laws, and precise citations—you will have a complete and rigorous proof of (x⋅y)⋅z = x⋅(y⋅z).

Your proof has the right overall idea—splitting into the trivial case \(a=0\) versus \(a\neq0\), then using the recursive law  
\[a\cdot\nu(c)=a\cdot c + a\]  
to force \(c=0\) and hence \(b=\nu(0)=1\).  In particular:  

• You correctly observe that if \(b=0\) then \(a\cdot b=0\), so \(a\cdot b=a\) forces \(a=0\).  
• You note that when \(a\neq0\) and \(b\neq0\), one has \(b=\nu(c)\) and so  
  \[a\cdot b \;=\;a\cdot\nu(c)\;=\;a\cdot c + a.\]  
  Demanding \(a\cdot c + a = a\) then “cancels” the final \(+\,a\) to deduce \(a\cdot c=0\), and from \(a\neq0\) conclude \(c=0\).

These are the key steps in a Peano‐style argument.  However, to make the reasoning fully rigorous you should:

1.  **Invoke the recursive definitions explicitly.**  When you write  
    \[a\cdot\nu(c)=a\cdot c+a,\]  
    you should cite the given axiom  
    \(\;x\cdot\nu(y)=x\cdot y + x.\)

2.  **Justify the “cancellation”**  
    Going from  
    \[a\cdot c + a = a\]  
    to  
    \[a\cdot c = 0\]  
    really uses the fact that addition by a nonzero summand cannot leave the other summand unchanged.  One way to see this is:  
    – Write \(a=\nu(a')\) since \(a\neq0\).  
    – Then \(a\cdot c + \nu(a') = \nu\bigl(a\cdot c + a'\bigr)\) by the recursion law for addition.  
    – By injectivity of \(\nu\) (Peano axiom P4), \(\nu(X)=\nu(Y)\) implies \(X=Y\).  Here you compare \(\nu(a\cdot c + a')\) with \(a=\nu(a')\) to get \(a\cdot c + a' = a'\), and then repeat if necessary or argue by induction on the second summand to deduce \(a\cdot c=0\).  

3.  **Streamline the case-analysis.**  
    You only need two main cases:  
    (i) \(a=0\) (then \(a\cdot b=0\)),  
    (ii) \(a\neq0\) (subdivide further into \(b=0\) and \(b\neq0\), with the latter giving \(b=\nu(c)\) and the above argument).  
    The extra paragraph starting “Other case: if \(b\neq1\)…” is somewhat redundant once you have the clean two-step analysis for \(b=0\) versus \(b=\nu(c)\).  

4.  **Mention the base‐case axiom for multiplication by zero.**  
    Early on you should cite  
    \[x\cdot 0 = 0,\]  
    to cover the \(b=0\) subcase.

With these additions—explicit citation of the recursive laws, a clear use of injectivity of \(\nu\) for cancellation, and a streamlined case-split—your proof will be fully aligned with the Peano framework.

\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
Addition is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x + 0 = x$ and $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x + \nu(y) = \nu(x+y)$\\
Multiplication is a binary operation on the natural numbers defined by the following properties. $\forall x \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot 0 = 0$ and  $\forall x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x \cdot \nu(y) = x \cdot y + x$.\\
worst_disagreements.feedback: The basic idea of the induction proof is there. However, the set $A$ is defined without explicit quantification over $y$, and $\nu(x) + y = \nu(x+y)$ as well as $0 + y = y$ for all $y \in \mathbb{N}$ are assumed without proof.
worst_disagreements.markscheme: 0/5 No steps link the Peano axioms or recursive definition to the claim, or the student appeals to unrelated results. 1/5 The answer may mention “if x+y=0 then x=0” or attempt a base‐case but invites invalid assumptions or misuses “successor” without a coherent logical framework. 2/5 One sees the right strategy—perhaps an induction on one summand or reference to “no predecessor of 0”—but the student omits proof of injectivity or of x+0=x, invoking non-trivial properties without justification. 3/5 A valid proof outline appears with base case and inductive step, yet key gaps remain (e.g. failing to show commutativity reduces y+ x=0 to x+y=0, or neglecting P3/P4 in the inductive argument). 4/5 A correct proof is given by induction and uses commutativity and Peano axioms; only minor details are glossed—perhaps the explicit verification of x+0=x or the injectivity step is left to the reader. 5/5 A fully rigorous, complete derivation invoking x+0=x, x+ν(y)=ν(x+y), commutativity, P3–P5 and injectivity yields x=0, y=0 with no logical leaps. worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Overall, you have the right high-level idea—use induction on one summand and the fact that no successor can equal 0—but the proof contains several gaps and mis‐applications of the Peano axioms.  Here are the main points to address:

1. Definition of your induction set  
   You define  
     A = { x∈ℕ | x+y=0 ⇒ x=0 and y=0 }  
   but this still “hides” the role of y inside your set.  It is clearer to fix an arbitrary y and prove  
     P(x) ≡ “x+y=0 ⇒ (x=0 and y=0)”  
   by induction on x alone.

2. Base case (x=0)  
   You write “Clearly 0+y=0⇒y=0 (A2),” presumably meaning from x+0=x or commutativity.  In fact you need:  
   – From commutativity, 0+y=y+0.  
   – From the recursive definition, y+0=y.  
   – So 0+y=0 ⇒ y=0.  
   Spell out these uses of commutativity and the defining axiom x+0=x.

3. Inductive step  
   You assume P(k) and try to show P(ν(k)).  Suppose for contradiction ν(k)+y=0.  By the recursive definition of addition,  
     ν(k)+y = ν(k + y).  
   So ν(k + y)=0.  Here you should invoke Peano axiom (P3), which says “no n satisfies ν(n)=0,” to get a contradiction.  You instead quoted (P4) and then asserted “ν(k)+y≠0 ⇒ y=0,” which does not follow.  Rather, the contradiction shows that ν(k)+y cannot be 0 at all, so there is no counterexample in the successor case.

4. Conclusion of induction  
   Having shown that no x>0 can satisfy x+y=0, you deduce that the only possibility is x=0—and from the base case we already know y=0.  Make that chain of reasoning explicit.

5. Optional remark on commutativity  
   If you prefer to prove “y+x=0⇒y=0” first and then swap arguments, you must either invoke commutativity of addition or rerun the same argument with roles of x and y exchanged.  

By addressing these points—defining the induction cleanly, spelling out uses of x+0=x and x+ν(y)=ν(x+y), using (P3) (not P4) to rule out ν(⋅)=0, and clearly concluding that x=0 forces y=0—you will reach a fully rigorous 5‐point solution.

worst_disagreements.markscheme: 0–5 marks will be awarded according to how completely and rigorously the student establishes the two implications “a∣b ⇒ each pᵢ appears among the qⱼ with at least the same exponent” and vice versa by exploiting uniqueness of prime factorization and the definition of divisibility.  A 5-mark answer gives a fully correct, logically watertight proof in both directions (possibly with only trivial notational lapses), a 4-mark answer is likewise essentially correct but omits or glosses over a small logical step, a 3-mark answer exhibits the right overall strategy (e.g. “if a∣b then b=ka so each pᵢ divides b so appears in its prime factorization,” and conversely) but leaves significant gaps or unproven assertions, a 2-mark answer uses the correct approach but relies on unestablished or non‐trivial properties without proof, a 1-mark answer contains only isolated relevant observations (e.g. recalling the definition of divisibility or stating the factorization theorem) without a coherent argument, and a 0-mark answer shows no meaningful engagement with the required prime‐factorization proof.  Throughout, full credit depends on the mathematical correctness and logical rigor of the argument rather than on perfect notation or exposition.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
You have identified the correct overall approach—using the uniqueness of prime factorizations in each direction—but the write-up leaves out the key exponent-counting arguments and does not show explicitly how to construct or decompose the witness \(k\).  In particular:

1. Backward direction (“if each \(p_i\) occurs among the \(q_j\) with \(s_j\ge r_i\), then \(a\mid b\)”):
   - You must define  
     \[
       k \;=\;\prod_{j=1}^n q_j^{\,s_j - \bigl(\text{exponent of }q_j\text{ in }a\bigr)},
     \]
     checking that each exponent \(s_j - (\cdots)\) is a nonnegative integer.  Then
     \[
       b \;=\;\prod_j q_j^{s_j}
         =\;\Bigl(\prod_j q_j^{(\cdots)}\Bigr)\;\times\;a
         =\;k\,a,
     \]
     so \(a\mid b\).  Your solution just states “rearranged to \(b=ka\)” without exhibiting \(k\) or verifying its exponents are nonnegative.

2. Forward direction (“if \(a\mid b\), then each \(p_i\) must appear among the \(q_j\) with at least exponent \(r_i\)”):
   - From \(b=ka\) and unique prime factorization, every prime factor of \(a\) (namely each \(p_i\)) must also appear in the factorization of \(b\).  You then need to compare exponents: in the product \(ka\) the total exponent of \(p_i\) is the sum of its exponents in \(k\) and in \(a\), so the exponent of \(p_i\) in \(b\) (namely \(s_j\)) must be at least \(r_i\).  This crucial step is only asserted, not shown.

Your solution correctly gestures at the right ideas but omits these exponent-counting details that make the proof watertight.  Fleshing out the construction of \(k\) in the backward direction and the exponent comparison in the forward direction will complete the argument.

worst_disagreements.feedback: Some correct elements: the idea to use the binomial formula is good. However the second $a-b \equiv 0\implies (a-b)^k \equiv 0$ is just assumed and not shown: this almost a circular argument. Induction over $k$ would have been a right way to go.
worst_disagreements.markscheme:
0/5: no use of the definition “a≡b mod n ⇔ n∣(a−b)”, no relevant ideas.  
1/5: recognizes a≡b ⇒ n∣(a−b) or that congruences multiply, but fails to extend this to k factors or misapplies the property.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof is headed in the right direction—using the binomial theorem is a standard way to show that every term except \(a^k\) and \(-b^k\) picks up a factor of \(n\). However, you have left out two key justifications:

1. Why does \(a\equiv b\pmod n\) imply \((a-b)^k\equiv 0\pmod n\)?  
   You need to say either “since \(n\mid(a-b)\), multiplying congruences (or taking powers) shows \(n\mid(a-b)^k\) and hence \((a-b)^k\equiv0\pmod n\).”

2. In your binomial‐theorem step you assert  
   \[
     (a-b)^k \;=\; a^k + nM - b^k
   \]  
   without explaining why each of the “middle” binomial terms is divisible by \(n\).  A clean way is to write \(a=b+nT\), expand
   \[
     (b+nT)^k = b^k + \binom{k}{1}b^{k-1}(nT) + \cdots + (nT)^k,
   \]
   and observe every term except \(b^k\) has a factor \(n\).

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
You’ve picked up on the right algebraic ideas—that if \(a<b\) you can write \(b=a+k\) with \(k\ge0\), and that multiplying or dividing by a positive number preserves inequalities—but the write‐up needs more care in invoking and applying the ordered‐field axioms and in handling strict versus non-strict inequalities. Here are a few concrete suggestions:

1. Forward implication:\  
   - You begin “\(a\le b\implies a+k=b\) for some \(k\ge0\).”  Since the problem asks for \(a<b\iff a^2<b^2\), you should start “if \(0<a<b\) then \(b-a>0\); write \(k=b-a\).”  
   - When you expand \((a+k)^2 = a^2 +2ak +k^2\), you need to say explicitly that \(k\ge0\) and \(a>0\) so \(2ak\ge0\) by Ordered-Field Axiom (O2), and \(k^2\ge0\) by the field axioms.  Hence \(a^2< a^2+2ak+k^2 = b^2\).  This shows \(a^2<b^2\).

2. Backward implication:\  
   - You assert “divide both sides by \(a\), so \(b/a\le b\).”  To be fully rigorous you must note that \(a>0\), so by (O2) you may multiply the inequality \(a^2<b^2\) by \(1/a\) (which exists by the field axioms) to get \(a < b^2/a\). 3. Axiom references and logical flow:\  
   - You need to invoke O2 each time you multiply or divide an inequality by a nonnegative or positive element.

worst_disagreements.prompt: Prove that the set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ is not bounded above in the reals.
worst_disagreements.feedback: The idea of the proof is correct, but the inequality $B+1 \geq B$ is insufficient to prove the point to be shown (we need $B+1 > B$). While fixing this is easy, the proof does also not show why precisely there is no upper bound of the natural numbers in the reals. This is not trivial, since there are non-archimedean ordered fields where indeed the natural numbers are bounded above.
worst_disagreements.markscheme: For this question the student’s work is scored out of 5 with the following emphasis: 0 points if there is no relevant attempt to show that ℕ has no real upper bound (e.g. no appeal to completeness, Archimedean property, or a construction producing n > M); 1 point if some correct idea appears (for instance mentioning “supremum” or “induction”) but the reasoning is invalid or mis‐applied; 2 points for a fundamentally correct approach (e.g. an outline invoking the least upper bound property or Archimedean argument) that nonetheless contains major unproved assumptions or logical gaps; 3 points for a valid proof route with notable imprecisions or omissions (such as failing to justify why s–1 cannot be an upper bound or glossing over the Archimedean step); 4 points for a substantially correct proof that establishes for arbitrary M ∈ ℝ a natural number exceeding M, with only minor logical steps omitted or trivial justifications elided; and 5 points for a fully rigorous, complete demonstration (via supremum contradiction, Archimedean principle, or integer‐part argument) free of substantive errors.  Throughout, the integrity and correctness of the mathematical argument take priority over notational neatness or stylistic clarity.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof correctly identifies the key idea—that if one assumes a “largest” natural number then adding one gives a contradiction—and this is a classic way to show there is no maximal element in ℕ. However, the question asks you to show that ℕ is not bounded above in ℝ, which is usually formulated as:

  “For every real number M, there exists n∈ℕ with n>M.”

Your argument shows “there is no largest natural number,” but it does not explicitly connect that fact to the statement about arbitrary real upper bounds.  To tighten it up, you could proceed in one of two ways:

1. Supremum‐contradiction route:  
   •  Suppose ℕ were bounded above in ℝ; then S = sup ℕ exists in ℝ.  
   •  By definition of supremum, S−1 cannot be an upper bound of ℕ, so ∃n∈ℕ with n>S−1, hence n+1>S.  
   •  But then n+1∈ℕ exceeds S, contradicting the fact that S is an upper bound.  

2. Archimedean (direct) route:  
   •  Let M be an arbitrary real.  
   •  Consider the usual inductive or ceiling‐function argument to produce an n∈ℕ with n>M (for example, take the least integer ≥M+1).  
   •  This shows directly that no real M can bound ℕ from above.

Either of these chains fills the gap in your proof by (a) starting with an arbitrary real M or (b) invoking the property of suprema, and thus establishes rigorously that ℕ has no real upper bound. The “add one” step in your proof is perfectly valid; just be sure to embed it in an argument that quantifies over all real candidates for an upper bound.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof shows you know that an inductive argument is needed and that you must use the recursive definitions and commutativity, but its logical structure is not clear and several key justifications are missing or mis-applied. In particular:

 1.  You never clearly state which variable you are inducting on (your “S” carries all three simultaneously without explaining an order) and you never give a standalone base case for that induction.  For example, if you induct on z you must begin with the base case
       (x+y)·0 = 0 = x·0 + y·0
     and say “assume for an arbitrary k that (x+y)·k = x·k + y·k,” before proving the step to ν(k).

 2.  In your “x-step” you write
       (ν(x)+y)·z = ν(x+y)·z = z·ν(x+y) 
     by commutativity, then conclude 
       = z·(x+y)+z = ν(x)·z + y·z.
     But you have not (i) said why ν(x+y)·z = z·ν(x+y) follows (you need commutativity of ·), (ii) shown how z·(x+y) + z becomes ν(x)·z + y·z (you must invoke the hypothesis (x,y,z)∈S to replace z·(x+y) by z·x+z·y, then reassociate), and (iii) justified that z·x + z = ν(x)·z by the definition of multiplication.

 3.  Your “y-step” simply appeals to commutativity of + but never explains how you carry the inductive hypothesis across, nor how the recursive definition of · is used.

 4.  In the “z-step” you assert 
       (x+y)·ν(z) = (x+y)·z + x + y
     without explicitly invoking the recursive definition of multiplication, and you then jump to 
       = x·ν(z) + y·ν(z)
     without spelling out the intermediate uses of the inductive hypothesis and the associativity/commutativity of +.

To repair the proof, pick one variable (say z) and do a clear two-part induction:

 •  Base Case (z=0):  
    Use x+0=x and x·0=0 to show (x+y)·0=0=x·0+y·0.

 •  Inductive Step (assume true for z=k):  
    Start with  
      (x+y)·ν(k) = (x+y)·k + (x+y)  (definition of ·)  
    = [x·k + y·k] + x + y           (inductive hypothesis)  
    = (x·k + x) + (y·k + y)         (re-associate using associativity/commutativity of +)  
    = x·ν(k) + y·ν(k)               (definition of · again).

Every use of “definition of ·,” “associativity,” or “commutativity” should be mentioned at the step where you apply it. That streamlined single induction on z, plus the commutativity of + to handle the symmetry in x,y, is enough to establish distributivity.

worst_disagreements.prompt:
Show that the number $0$ does not have a predecessor in $\mathbb{N}$ assuming only the Peano axioms and the definition of a predecessor: $x,y \in \mathbb{N}, x$ is a predecessor of $y$ if $\nu(x) = y$.
The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof correctly identifies the right ideas (surjectivity from “every nonzero has a predecessor,” injectivity from “that predecessor is unique,” and the inverse as the successor), but it is too much of a sketch and does not actually deploy the Peano axioms or check the necessary domain‐and‐codomain restrictions.  Here is what you need to add to make it fully rigorous:

1. Surjectivity (using P3 and the definition of π):  
   – You must show: for every m∈ℕ there is n∈ℕ∖{0} with π(n)=m.  
   – Argument: given m∈ℕ, consider n≔ν(m).  By P3, ν(m)≠0, so n lies in the domain ℕ∖{0}.  By the definition of π, π(n)=π(ν(m))=m.  This exactly shows π is onto ℕ.

2. Injectivity (using P4):  
   – You must show: if π(a)=π(b) then a=b, for a,b∈ℕ∖{0}.  
   – Argument: π(a)=π(b) implies ν(π(a))=ν(π(b)).  But by the definition of π, ν(π(a))=a and ν(π(b))=b, so a=b.  Here you invoke P4 (the injectivity of ν).

3. Domain and codomain bookkeeping:  
   – State clearly that π:ℕ∖{0}→ℕ is defined by “π(x) is the unique y with ν(y)=x.”  
   – Observe by P3 that ν(y) never equals 0, so 0∉Im ν, which is why π’s domain omits 0.  
   – Then note that the inverse π⁻¹ must go from ℕ back to ℕ∖{0}.

4. Explicit inverse function:  
   – Define π⁻¹(m):=ν(m), with m∈ℕ.  
   – Check that π⁻¹ is well‐defined into ℕ∖{0} (again by P3, ν(m)≠0).  
   – Verify π⁻¹(π(x))=ν(π(x))=x and π(π⁻¹(m))=π(ν(m))=m.

By spelling out each of these steps and citing the relevant axioms (P3 for “ν(m)≠0,” P4 for injectivity of ν, and the uniqueness of predecessors built into the definition of π), your proof will achieve the full rigor expected under the Peano framework.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof has the right overall strategy—induction on z with the base case and an inductive step using the recursive definition of multiplication—but it leaves some important gaps and contains an algebraic slip. Here are some points to tighten:

1. Base case  
   – You correctly observe that for every fixed x,y,  
     (x+y)·0 = 0 = x·0 + y·0  
     by the definition x·0 = 0. No further justification is needed here.

2. Inductive step  
   – You start from the inductive hypothesis  
     (x+y)·z = x·z + y·z.  
   – You then write  
     (x+y)·ν(z) = (x+y)·z + (x+y)  
     by the defining clause for multiplication. Good.  
   – Next you invoke your IH to get  
     (x+y)·z + (x+y) = (x·z + y·z) + (x+y).  
     At this point you need to explain two things explicitly:  
     a) that you are applying the IH to replace (x+y)·z by x·z + y·z;  
     b) that you are using associativity and commutativity of + to regroup  
        (x·z + y·z) + (x+y) into (x·z + x) + (y·z + y).  
   – In your write-up you have a typo “+…+y·z+z” instead of “+y·z+y.” That obscures the logic. The correct regrouping is  
     (x·z + x) + (y·z + y) = x·ν(z) + y·ν(z)  
     once you use the defining clause x·ν(z) = x·z + x (and similarly for y).

3. Justification of commutativity/associativity  
   – You have appealed to commutativity (and implicitly associativity) of addition. Since the exercise asked you to work entirely from the Peano axioms and the recursive definitions, you should at least note that these properties themselves require separate proofs by induction. If you do want to use them, say explicitly “by associativity and commutativity of + (each provable by a prior induction).”

4. Use of Peano’s fifth axiom  
   – You invoked P5 (induction) correctly. For full rigor you might restate: “Since 0∈S and z∈S ⇒ ν(z)∈S, by P5 we conclude S = ℕ.” But the idea is there.

Summary of what to fix  
– Correct the algebraic typo in the inductive step (+y, not +z).  
– Spell out each application of a definition or prior result: the IH, the recursive laws for ·, and the laws for +.  
– Acknowledge (or briefly justify) where associativity/commutativity of + is used, since these are not primitive Peano axioms but theorems themselves.

With these adjustments, your proof will be fully rigorous under the Peano framework.

worst_disagreements.prompt: \ Let $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Show that if $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}$ for all $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ then $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your argument correctly observes that the hypothesis gives  
 for each basis vector bᵢ, u·bᵢ = v·bᵢ,  
but it stops short of a valid inference that u and v then share all coordinates.  In fact, unless {bᵢ} is assumed orthonormal, the dot‐product u·bᵢ does *not* in general equal the i-th coordinate of u.  As stated, “arbitrary basis” is too weak to justify “all their components are the same.”  

To complete the proof you need one of two routes:

1.  **Orthonormal‐basis approach.**  First note (or assume) that you may choose an *orthonormal* basis {eᵢ}.  Then indeed u·eᵢ (and v·eᵢ) is the i-th coordinate of u (respectively v), so u·eᵢ = v·eᵢ for all i forces u = v.

2.  **Difference‐vector approach (more standard).**  Set d = u−v.  By bilinearity,  
 d·w = (u−v)·w = u·w − v·w = 0 for *all* w.  
Now choose w = d to get d·d = ‖d‖² = 0, and invoke positive-definiteness of the dot product to conclude d = 0, hence u = v.

Either method, carried out with a clear justification of why u·eᵢ picks out components or why ‖d‖² = 0 forces d = 0, yields a complete proof.

worst_disagreements.prompt: Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$, $d=gcd(a,b)$ and consider the equation $ax+by=c$. Show that if $d|c$ and the equation $ax+by=c$ has one integer solution $(x_0,y_0)\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$, then it has infinitely many integer solutions.

worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof shows you know that Bézout’s lemma guarantees a particular solution when \(d=\gcd(a,b)\) divides \(c\). However, the argument for “infinitely many” solutions is too sketchy: you never exhibit the standard one‐parameter family of solutions, and your phrases “add \(d\) to \(x\)” and “take away \(dx\) by finding the change in coefficients” are not precise enough to persuade the reader.

Here is what you need to do to complete the proof:

1.  **Start from one known solution.**  
    The hypothesis says there is at least one integer solution \((x_0,y_0)\) to 
    \[
      a x + b y = c.
    \]
    You don’t have to re‐derive that solution via Bézout’s lemma—just call it \((x_0,y_0)\).

2.  **Use the standard parameter shift.**  
    Set \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\) and define
    \[
      x(t)=x_0+\frac{b}{d}\,t,
      \quad
      y(t)=y_0-\frac{a}{d}\,t.
    \]
    Since \(a\bigl(\tfrac{b}{d}\bigr)-b\bigl(\tfrac{a}{d}\bigr)=0,\) you check immediately that
    \[
      a\,x(t)+b\,y(t)
      =a x_0+b y_0
      +t\Bigl(a\frac{b}{d}-b\frac{a}{d}\Bigr)
      =c.
    \]
    Because \(a/d\) and \(b/d\) are integers, each \((x(t),y(t))\) is integral. And as \(t\) varies over all of \(\mathbb{Z}\), you produce infinitely many *distinct* solutions.

3.  **Conclude.**  
    This one‐parameter family shows there cannot be only finitely many integer solutions.

By spelling out steps 1–3 you give a clear, complete proof. In particular, the key points you were missing were:  
•  Emphasis that you already *have* one solution \((x_0,y_0)\).  
•  The explicit parameterization \((x_0 + (b/d)t,\;y_0 - (a/d)t)\).  
•  A check that this indeed gives infinitely many *integer* solutions.

Once this is laid out, the argument is both rigorous and easy to follow.

The Peano axioms state the following properties about $\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}
[(P1)] There exists a distinguished element $0 \in \mathbb{N}$.
[(P2)] There exists a map $\nu : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ called the successor map.
[(P3)] There exists no element $n$ such that $\nu(n) = 0$.
[(P4)] The map $\nu$ is injective, i.e. for all $n_1, n_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, if $n_1 \neq n_2$, then $\nu(n_1) \neq \nu(n_2)$.
[(P5)] Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such that $0 \in A$ and $\nu(n) \in A$ for all $n \in A$, then $A = \mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}
worst_disagreements.output:
\begin{proof}
Existence of a predecessor: \\
Base Case: 1 has a predecessor, namely 0.\\
Induction Hypothesis: some non-zero natural number, $n$, has a predecessor.\\
Then $\nu(n)$ has a predecessor in the natural numbers, it is $n$. Then by induction (the fifth Peano axiom) all non-zero natural numbers have a predecessor in $\mathbb{N}$.\\
Uniqueness of a predecessor:\\
Let $x$ be an arbitrary non-zero element in $\mathbb{N}$ which has two distinct predecessors. That is $\exists a, b \in \mathbb{N} $ with $ a \neq b$ and $ \nu(a) = \nu(b) = x$ but Peano's axioms define the successor function to be injective so this is a contradiction.
\end{proof}
worst_disagreements.feedback: The student uses induction somehow correctly. However the set over which the induction is done is not defined. Uniqueness is proved correctly.
worst_disagreements.llm_feedback:
Your proof captures the right ideas—using induction (axiom P5) for existence and injectivity (P4) for uniqueness—and you have identified the correct “base‐case” and “inductive‐step.”  To sharpen it a bit, here are a few suggestions:

1.  Be explicit about what “1” means.  
    •  In the Peano framework one usually defines  
       1 := ν(0).  
    •  Then the base case is: since 1 = ν(0), 1’s predecessor is 0.

2.  Spell out the induction argument in the style of axiom P5.  For existence you want to show:  
    Let 
      A = { m ∈ ℕ : m = 0 or ∃k with ν(k) = m }.  
    •  Check 0 ∈ A (trivially).  
    •  Show “if n ∈ A then ν(n) ∈ A.”  
         –  If n = 0, then ν(n)=1=ν(0), so ν(n) has a predecessor.  
         –  If n=ν(k), then ν(n)=ν(ν(k)), so again ν(n) has a predecessor (namely ν(k)).  
    By P5 we conclude A = ℕ, so every nonzero n is in the image of ν and hence has at least one predecessor.

3.  The uniqueness part is perfectly concise: if ν(a) = ν(b) = x then by injectivity (P4) a = b.

Overall you have all the right ingredients.  Just be sure to  
  •  Define 1 as ν(0),  
  •  Describe the set you apply induction to,  
  •  Check both cases in the inductive step,  
and your proof will be fully rigorous and self-contained.
