Your write-up correctly identifies the heart of the matter: π really is a bijection from ℕ∖{0} onto ℕ, and its inverse is the successor map ν. You get full credit for spotting that and for splitting the argument into surjectivity and injectivity.  

Here are a few suggestions to make your proof more precise and to show explicitly how the Peano axioms are at work:

1.  Surjectivity  
    –  Goal: show ∀ n∈ℕ ∃ x∈ℕ∖{0} so that π(x)=n.  
    –  More concretely, for each n take x:=ν(n). By Peano axiom (P2) ν(n)∈ℕ, and by (P3) ν(n)≠0, so indeed x∈ℕ∖{0}. Then by definition of π, π(ν(n))=n.  
    –  This exhibits an explicit preimage for every n∈ℕ, making the surjectivity argument crystal-clear.

2.  Injectivity  
    –  Goal: show if π(x₁)=π(x₂) then x₁=x₂.  
    –  By the “uniqueness of predecessor” hypothesis (which follows from (P4) plus the definition of π), any given y has at most one x with ν(x)=y.  Thus if π(x₁)=y=π(x₂), then ν(x₁)=y=ν(x₂), so x₁=x₂.

3.  Concluding Bijectivity  
    –  Since you have both surjectivity and injectivity, π is a bijection ℕ∖{0}→ℕ.

4.  Identifying the Inverse  
    –  You assert correctly that the inverse π⁻¹ must go from ℕ back to ℕ∖{0}, and that π⁻¹(n)=ν(n).  
    –  You can check directly: for every n∈ℕ,  
       •  (π∘ν)(n)=π(ν(n))=n,  
       •  for every m∈ℕ∖{0}, (ν∘π)(m)=ν(π(m))=m.  
    –  These two compositions being the respective identity maps show ν is indeed π’s inverse.

5.  Minor Points  
    –  Watch your wording: you wrote “all non-negative integers have a unique predecessor,” but the domain of π is ℕ∖{0}, so you mean “all positive (i.e.\ nonzero) naturals have a unique predecessor.”  
    –  Whenever you invoke existence or uniqueness, tie it back to exactly which Peano axiom or definition you are using (P2 for the successor map, P3 for ν(n)≠0, P4 for injectivity of ν, and the given uniqueness-of-predecessor property).

Overall you have the right ideas in place.  By spelling out the explicit preimages for surjectivity, the exact injectivity-by-uniqueness argument, and the two composition checks, you will have a fully rigorous proof meeting the expected learning goals.

Here is some feedback on your write‐up. I’ll organize it around the main proof‐technique you chose (induction), the logical gaps I see, and a few suggestions for tightening up the argument.

1. Overall strategy  
   • You propose a “double induction” on x and y, which is indeed the standard approach for showing ∀ x,y∈ℕ: x+y = y+x.  
   • In fact one can cleanly do a single induction on y, with an inner proof “for all x” that itself uses induction on x when needed.  

2. Base case(s)  
   – You correctly point out that for y=0 the statement becomes “for all x: x+0 = 0+x.”  This is a crucial base step.  
   – You refer to a result from lecture notes that x+0 = 0+x.  If that lemma has already been proved from the Peano axioms, then it is perfectly fine to invoke it here.  However, you should (a) state exactly how that lemma was proved, and (b) run through the induction on x if the lemma itself was established by induction—so that your write-up stands alone.  

3. Inductive step on y  
   – You assume as induction hypothesis IH(y) that for this particular y, ∀ x: x+y = y+x.  Good.  
   – You then consider x+ν(y) and immediately write  
        x+ν(y) = ν(x+y)   (by the recursive definition of +)  
                 = ν(y+x)   (by IH(y))  
                 = ν(y)+x   (…here is where a gap appears.)  

4. The missing lemma: “ν(y)+x = ν(y+x)”  
   • The recursive definition of addition only tells you how to handle the second argument:  
       a+0 = a, a+ν(b) = ν(a+b).  
     It does *not* directly give you a formula for ν(y)+x, unless you do a further (inner) induction on x.  
   • In other words, to transform ν(y+x) into ν(y)+x you need to prove for every fixed y the auxiliary claim  
        ∀ x ν(y)+x = ν(y+x).  
     And that auxiliary claim is exactly what one proves by induction on x, using the same two equations for +.  

5. How to patch it with nested induction  
   A more streamlined proof might look like this:  
   – Outer induction on y: prove P(y): “for all x, x+y = y+x.”  
     • Base y=0: Prove P(0)—i.e. x+0 = 0+x—for all x, by a short induction on x if necessary (or by your prior lemma).  
     • Step y→ν(y): Assume P(y).  You must show ∀x: x+ν(y) = ν(y)+x.  Now for each x do an inner induction:  
         · Inner base x=0: 0+ν(y) = ν(0+y) = ν(y) by defn, and ν(y)+0 = ν(y) by defn.  
         · Inner step x→ν(x): assume x+ν(y)=ν(y)+x and show ν(x)+ν(y)=ν(y)+ν(x).  Both sides expand by the recursive rule on the second argument.  

6. Presentation tips  
   • Be explicit about which variable you are inducting on—state “Fix y and we induct on x” or vice versa.  
   • Clearly label your base cases and inductive hypotheses.  
   • If you rely on a lemma from lecture, either re-state it briefly or indicate that its proof is elsewhere in your notes.  
   • Avoid the phrase “which holds ∀x∈ℕ” without showing how the quantifier interacts with your induction steps.

  + You have identified the right overall technique (induction on both variables).  
  – You need to fill in the auxiliary induction that justifies the step ν(y+x) = ν(y)+x.  
  – Your write-up would benefit from a clearer, two‐level structure: an outer induction on y, plus an inner induction on x only in the inductive step.  
  – Make sure every use of the Peano axioms or of previously proved lemmas is explicitly cited or reproved, so the argument is self-contained.

        • Suppose ℕ were bounded above. Then by completeness it has a supremum L. Show that L–1 is still an upper bound for ℕ, a contradiction.

   b) Use of absolute values:  
     – You introduce |·| in the definition of S, but the statement you want is simply “nx>y.”  Since x>0, you can streamline by working directly with nx and y (no need to juggle |nx| and |y|).

   c) Clarity of quantifiers and negation:  
     – When negating “∃ n with nx>y” you should write “∀ n, nx ≤ y.”  Your write-up says “S = ℕ ⇒ n < |y/x|,” but it’s really “for each n, n ≤ |y|/x.”  Be explicit:

     • Suppose for contradiction that for every n∈ℕ we have n x ≤ y.

You’ve correctly identified the central idea—considering the quadratic polynomial  
   P(λ) = (u + λv)·(u + λv)  
and using the fact that P(λ) ≥ 0 for all real λ to force the discriminant to be non‐positive.  From that you extract  
   (u·v)² ≤ (u·u)(v·v),  
which is exactly the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.  This is precisely the approach we discussed in class, so you’re on the right track.  

Here are a few suggestions to tighten up the presentation and clear up small errors:

1.  **Write out P(λ) carefully.**  
    Your expansion should read  
       P(λ) = u·u  +  2λ (u·v)  +  λ² (v·v).  
    In your write‐up the middle term lost its factor of λ.  

2.  **Explain the link to the discriminant.**  
    You wrote “it can have at most one (repeated) real solution, due to inner products yielding results ≥0.”  A clearer way is:  
    – Since P(λ) ≥ 0 for every real λ, the quadratic cannot change sign, so it cannot have two distinct real roots.  
    – Equivalently, the discriminant Δ = [2(u·v)]² − 4(u·u)(v·v) must satisfy Δ ≤ 0.  

3.  **Be precise about absolute values.**  
    After you derive (u·v)² ≤ (u·u)(v·v), you can immediately take square roots to get  
       |u·v| ≤ √(u·u) √(v·v) = |u| |v|.  

4.  **Equality‐case computations.**  
    – If u = k v then u·v = k (v·v), so |u·v| = |k| |v|², while |u||v| = |k||v|² as well.  
    – Conversely, when Δ = 0 there is a unique real root λ₀ = −(u·v)/(v·v), and P(λ₀) = 0 forces u + λ₀ v = 0, i.e. u is a scalar multiple of v.  This shows the “if and only if” neatly.  

5.  **Minor remark on the zero‐vector case.**  
    If either u or v is 0, both sides of the inequality are zero and the equality condition holds trivially; it’s often worth mentioning this as a special (but immediate) case.

Overall, you have the right high‐level strategy and obtained the correct inequality.  Polishing the algebraic details—especially keeping track of λ in the cross term, using absolute values cleanly, and spelling out the discriminant argument—will make your proof completely rigorous and crystal clear.

First, assume $\mathbf{u} = k\mathbf{v}$, then $|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| = (k\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v})(k\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = k^2(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = (k\mathbf{v} \cdot k\mathbf{v})(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u})(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v})$.The equality is satisfied. \\
Now to show the other direction. Assume that $(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u})(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v})$, then the discriminant of $P(\lambda) = 0$ so the polynomial has a real root. Therefore, $\exists \lambda$ such that $(\mathbf{u} + \lambda\mathbf{v}) = 0$, proving that the two vectors are linearly dependent.
\end{proof}

Here is the student’s proof with inline annotations.  Real mistakes are marked in red, minor slips in yellow, and helpful comments in green.

\begin{proof}
Let \(a, b, c\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy 
\[
\cos a + \cos b + \cos c = 0,\quad
\sin a + \sin b + \sin c = 0.
\]
Then 
\[
e^{i a} + e^{i b} + e^{i c} = 0.
\]
\textcolor{green}{Good step: combining sines and cosines into one complex equation.}

Equivalently, \(e^{i a},e^{i b},e^{i c}\) are the affixes of the vertices of an equilateral triangle centered at the origin.  
\textcolor{yellow}{Saying “\(a,b,c\) are affixes” is a slip—really the points \(e^{i a},e^{i b},e^{i c}\) are.}  
Hence we may, up to rotation, set
\[
b = a + \tfrac{2\pi}{3},\qquad
c = a + \tfrac{4\pi}{3}.
\]
\textcolor{green}{One should mention “up to reordering and adding multiples of \(2\pi\).”}

Then
\[
e^{i a} + e^{i b} + e^{i c}
= e^{i a}\,\bigl(1 + e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}} + e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}}\bigr)
= 0,
\]
since \(1+e^{i2\pi/3}+e^{i4\pi/3}=0\).

Squaring both sides gives
\[
\bigl[e^{i a}\,(1 + e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}} + e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}})\bigr]^2
= 0.
\]
\textcolor{yellow}{Be careful to square the correct sum: it remains \(1+e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}}+e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}}\), not twice one term.}

Thus
\[
e^{2i a}\,\bigl(1 + e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}} + e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}}\bigr)^2
=0
\;\implies\;
e^{2i a}\,(1 + e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}} + e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}})
=0
\]
\textcolor{green}{Division by \(1 + e^{i2\pi/3} + e^{i4\pi/3}\neq0\) is justified since that sum is zero only once (we used it above).}

Hence
\[
e^{2i a} + e^{2i b} + e^{2i c}
= e^{2i a} + e^{2i(a+\tfrac{2\pi}{3})} + e^{2i(a+\tfrac{4\pi}{3})}
= 0.
\]
Equating real and imaginary parts yields
\[
\cos2a + \cos2b + \cos2c = 0,\quad
\sin2a + \sin2b + \sin2c = 0,
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

Summary of issues:
- \textcolor{yellow}{Mixed up “angles” \(a,b,c\) with the “affixes” \(e^{i a},e^{i b},e^{i c}\).}  
- \textcolor{red}{A typo when squaring: you wrote the \(e^{i2\pi/3}\) term twice.}  
- \textcolor{green}{Nice idea using complex exponentials and symmetry to reduce to the \(120^\circ\) case.}

worst_disagreements.prompt:
\ $N(>2)$ dogs are equidistantly distributed on the circumference of a circle of radius $R$. Suddenly, at $t = 0$, the dogs enter a race where each chases his nearest (counter-clockwise) neighbour. Assume that for $t > 0$ each dog runs at a constant speed $v$ at a heading always directly towards its neighbour.
Will the dogs ever catch up with each other? If so, what distance will they traverse before
doing so?
worst_disagreements.output:
\begin{proof}
Due to the dogs being equidistant from each other, we use the symmetry principle to determine that the position of the dogs will form an equilateral triangle of which the center will be the center of the original circle since the dogs will stay equidistant due to symmetry and distance from the center will be the same for all the dogs. \\
From this, we see the dogs will meet at the center if they do indeed meet. We now only need to consider the distance each dog is from the center. \\
Since each dog is travelling at speed $v$ towards each other, we take the component of speed in the direction of the center. \\
Due to results from Trigonometry, this is $\frac{v \sqrt{3}}{2} $.
Our speed is constant, so time until dogs reach the center is $\frac{2R}{v \sqrt{3}}$
\end{proof}
worst_disagreements.feedback: Elements of a correct solution are there, i.e. the notion that symmetry properties of the problem allow us to conclude that the configuration of the $N$ dogs will always be a regular $N$-gon and that describing the motion in polar coordinates shows that the $N$-gon shrinks at a constant rate dependent only on the angular separation of the dogs and speed (hence only on $N$ and $v$), showing both convergence to the center and time/distance to convergence. However, these arguments are not clearly laid out in the proposed solution and the solution only treats the case $N=3$.
